subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
Monday: In the weekly review at the logistics office, Hemant went pale when the regional manager asked about the missing consignment, and his hands shook as he turned the pages. Santosh leaned over and whispered, "Relax, yaar, she won't eat you." Hemant didn't smile.
Wednesday: Santosh found Hemant gripping the photocopier, face grey, sweat on his upper lip. This time Santosh didn't joke. "Hey, are you okay? Do you want to sit? Water? Should I call someone?" Hemant sank into a chair and said he had skipped breakfast and lunch and felt dizzy. Santosh fetched the office first-aider and a packet of biscuits and stayed with him until the colour came back.
The following Monday: Hemant said a doctor had checked him and he now kept food in his drawer. Santosh thought back to that first review. He had been so sure it was nerves. It might have been hunger all along.

qa.q: Who did Santosh fetch on Wednesday along with a packet of biscuits?
qa.a: Santosh fetched the office first-aider.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling the following Monday when he thought back to the first review?
qa.a: Santosh likely felt uneasy and a little embarrassed that he had been so sure Hemant was nervous, when hunger might have caused the paleness.

qa.q: What went right on Wednesday, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Santosh checked on Hemant's safety first, offered a seat, water or a call, and stayed with him, so a possible health problem was handled before anyone judged emotions.

qa.q: What might Hemant have felt when Santosh joked "she won't eat you" on Monday?
qa.a: Hemant may have felt brushed off and unseen, especially if he was feeling faint rather than scared of the manager.

grounding: Shows that a colleague's sudden paleness or shaking may come from illness or hunger as well as fear, so checking health and safety comes first.

passage: Binita's phone buzzed with her brother's angry voice note about the quarrel over the family field boundary, just as the call from the buyer in Pune came through. Her jaw was tight. In the tin-roofed cooperative office near Sangli, with hens scratching outside the door, she rolled her shoulders, put on the warm voice she kept for buyers and smiled so it would reach her words. "Namaskar, Mehra-ji! Yes, the ghee shipment leaves Friday. We're very glad to have your order again." The buyer laughed and added twenty tins. When the call ended, Binita let the smile drop. Abhinav, who kept the accounts at the next desk, looked up. "You sounded happy." "I chose to sound happy," she said. "I'm actually furious with my brother." She stepped out, walked to the well and back, and then called her brother to talk it through in her ordinary voice.

qa.q: What shipment did Binita say would leave on Friday?
qa.a: The ghee shipment would leave Friday.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling while she spoke warmly to the buyer?
qa.a: Binita was furious with her brother after the voice note but chose a warm voice on purpose; the tight jaw showed the anger was still there under the smile.

qa.q: Which part of Binita's handling was healthy, and why?
qa.a: The warm voice for the buyer was an ordinary work skill, and she also named the anger to Abhinav and took a walk, so the feeling was not simply buried.

qa.q: How might Abhinav read Binita's cheerful calls if she never explained?
qa.a: Abhinav might believe she was always genuinely happy and miss the times she needed a moment, which could lead him to misjudge her mood.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional choosing a warm display for a client call on purpose while still acknowledging the real feeling afterwards.

subtype: Literal, figurative and posed communication at work [Interpreting]
passage: The email from Pallavi arrived at 9:02: "Loved the deck. Very bold choices on slide 4. 🔥" Divyansh read it three times at his desk in the Gurugram office. Bold as in brave, or bold as in too much? His teammate Rhea leaned over. "Fire means she's roasting you," she said. "Or it means it's hot. Who knows." Divyansh started typing a defensive reply about why the orange background matched the client's colours, then stopped. Last week Pallavi had written "Can we take a stab at a shorter version?" and he had spent a whole night cutting slides when she had meant two minutes of trimming. He walked over to her cabin instead. "Quick check on slide 4. When you said bold, did you mean it works, or it's too loud?" Pallavi laughed. "It works! I just want the font a size smaller so the client can read it from the back." Divyansh went back and changed one setting.

qa.q: What did Pallavi want changed on slide 4?
qa.a: Pallavi wanted the font a size smaller so the client could read it from the back.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh stop typing the defensive reply, and what was he feeling?
qa.a: Divyansh felt anxious and defensive about "bold choices", but remembered losing a night over "take a stab", so he doubted his first reading and chose to check.

qa.q: What could Divyansh keep doing when a work message feels unclear?
qa.a: Ask a short, specific question about what the writer meant, as he did at Pallavi's cabin, before reacting to a guess.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt if she had received the defensive reply?
qa.a: Pallavi might have been confused and a little hurt, since she meant the fire emoji as praise, and a simple font request could have turned into a needless argument.

grounding: Shows a young professional unsure whether a remark is literal, figurative or sarcastic, and checking intent instead of assuming.

passage: I'm Abhinav, and I lead a small support team in Hyderabad. Last week I told Tushar, in front of our visiting client, that his account was moving to a newer colleague. He smiled, nodded twice and said, "Of course, whatever works best for the team." The client beamed. I almost ticked it off as agreed. But I had seen Tushar's pen clicking under the table, and the smile stayed fixed long after the topic changed. In his family, I knew, you never argued with seniors in front of guests. Still, I couldn't be sure what he felt. After the client left, I found him at the water cooler. "Tushar, I sprang that on you in public. Is it really okay, or would you rather talk it through?" He hesitated. "Honestly, it stung. I've built that account for two years." We sat down and worked out a handover he could live with.

qa.q: What did Tushar say when he heard his account was moving?
qa.a: Tushar said, "Of course, whatever works best for the team."

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling behind his fixed smile?
qa.a: Tushar was hurt and upset about losing an account built over two years; the clicking pen hinted at it, although to the client the smile looked like agreement.

qa.q: What did Abhinav try that cleared up the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Abhinav spoke to Tushar privately, owned that the news was sprung in public, and asked directly whether it was really okay, which let Tushar say it stung.

qa.q: How did the visiting client probably read Tushar's smile?
qa.a: The client likely took the smile and nods as happy agreement, with no idea that Tushar was upset.

grounding: Shows a young adult smiling politely out of respect while upset, and how a gentle direct question stops it being mistaken for agreement.

passage: In the staff room of a Jaipur secondary school, Kashish clicked to her Class 8 attendance chart and the projector showed a recipe for aloo paratha instead. Twelve teachers stared at it. Kashish burst out laughing, too loud and too long. "Oh my god, I'm such a disaster, ha ha, don't mind me, I'm hopeless with laptops!" She kept laughing while she scrolled, cheeks burning, and people began to shift in their chairs. Vinita, the vice principal, waited quietly. Kashish caught her calm look and took a breath. "Sorry, my mistake, wrong file. Here's the right one." She opened the chart. "Attendance dropped on Mondays in October. I'd like to try a Monday morning quiz to pull it back up." Two teachers nodded and started writing. Afterwards, Vinita stopped by her chair. "That second minute was much stronger than the first." Kashish let out a shaky breath and smiled.

qa.q: What appeared on the projector instead of the Class 8 attendance chart?
qa.a: A recipe for aloo paratha appeared instead.

qa.q: What does Kashish's loud, long laugh suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Mostly embarrassment, shown by her burning cheeks, mixed with hope that laughing would ease the tension; it could also have been nervous surprise at the wrong file.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Laughing it off and calling herself hopeless kept the attention on the mistake; owning it briefly with "wrong file" and moving on to the Monday quiz got the meeting back on track.

qa.q: How might the other teachers have felt during the long laugh?
qa.a: They were likely uncomfortable, shifting in their chairs and unsure whether to laugh along or look away, until Kashish moved on 😅

grounding: Illustrates a young professional laughing after a mistake in a meeting, then owning the error briefly and moving on as the steadier choice.

subtype: Smiling while crying, tears of joy [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Uma, and I was handing out marigold garlands at my cousin Ganga's wedding when I saw it. The shehnai started for the pheras, and Ganga's face did two things at once. She was smiling so wide her cheeks lifted, and tears were rolling straight down into her dupatta. Her hands trembled on the edge of the mandap. Guests near me whispered. One aunty said, "Nerves." Another said, "Must be missing her father." I didn't know which, or if it was something else. Later, during the photos, I slipped beside her with a tissue. "Happy tears? Or would you like a minute?" She squeezed my hand. "Both. I'm so happy. And Papa would have loved this music." I didn't say anything wise. I just held her hand while the photographer counted to three, and we both smiled through it.

qa.q: What was Uma handing out at the wedding?
qa.a: Uma was handing out marigold garlands.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling as she smiled and cried at the pheras?
qa.a: Ganga felt joy at her wedding and grief that Papa was not there to hear the music, both at once; only asking showed it was both.

qa.q: What made Uma's response helpful?
qa.a: Uma offered a tissue and a simple question, happy tears or a minute alone, then just held Ganga's hand instead of explaining the feelings away 🤍

qa.q: Why might the guests have read Ganga's tears differently from each other?
qa.a: Each guest saw the same smiling tears but brought a different guess, nerves or missing her father, because a mixed display does not show its cause from outside.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult crying and smiling at once at a wedding, and a listener who simply asks and shares the moment.
